title: Delivering Work Faster with Prompt Templates

thumbnail.headline: Write Once, Reuse Forever
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a single recipe-style card with five labelled lines and a teal bookmark, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Write Once, Reuse Forever
slide.body: One recipe-style card with five short labelled lines (Role, Task, Inputs, Format, Rules) and a teal bookmark tab. Small tag: AI for Freelancers · Lesson 6.

production_notes: The curriculum's '60 to 80 percent' illustration was removed in Stage 2 and must not return in any caption or graphic. The script tells learners to measure time on their own work. Do not add any 'percent saved' figure.
Mateus's times (about 10 minutes for the draft, about 35 minutes checking) are hypothetical and described as his own measurement.
Mateus and his six clients are fictional. Any on-screen report must use invented figures and no real business or social media account names.

Hook.voiceover: If you type a new prompt every time you need a report, you get a different result every time. The freelancers who save the most time do not write better prompts each day. They write good prompts once, and reuse them.

Explain.voiceover: Last time, you built an onboarding pack. Today, we move to the delivery stage, and make your routine client work faster and more consistent.

slide.title: Delivering Work Faster with Prompt Templates
slide.body: AI for Freelancers and Solopreneurs · Lesson 6 of 12

Explain.voiceover: A prompt template is a saved prompt with fixed instructions and blanks that you fill in for each client. A good template has five parts. A role and context. The task. The inputs, which are the blanks you fill in. The format, such as length, headings and tone. And rules, such as do not invent figures.

slide.title: Five parts of a template
slide.body: 1 Role and context · 2 Task · 3 Inputs: [CLIENT TYPE] [DATA] [KEY POINTS] · 4 Format: length, headings, tone · 5 Rules: do not invent figures; mark anything uncertain with [CHECK]

Explain.voiceover: Start with your most common deliverables. First drafts, research notes, design briefs or monthly reports. Test each template three times with different example inputs, and improve it when the output is weak.

slide.title: Test and improve
slide.body: Loop: Write template → Test with example input 1, 2, 3 → Spot weak output → Improve → back to Test

Explain.voiceover: How much time will you save? It varies a lot by task, by trade, and by how good your inputs are. So do not rely on any general figure. Measure it on your own work, including the time you spend checking. What stays with you is the part clients pay for. The expert decisions, the judgement about what matters, and the final check.

Think of a recipe card in a busy restaurant kitchen. The chef does not invent the sauce again every evening. The recipe gives the same good base each time. But the chef still tastes it and adjusts it before the plate leaves the kitchen.
Explain.stock_query: chef tasting sauce in restaurant kitchen

Explain.voiceover: Keep your templates in one document, each with a name, the date you last changed it, and an example of good output. And never put real client secrets or personal data into the inputs. Use summaries or anonymised figures instead.

slide.title: Your template library
slide.body: One document · Name · Date last changed · Example of good output · Inputs: summaries or anonymised figures only

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's look at an example. Mateus is a social media consultant in Porto Alegre, Brazil. Every month, he writes a performance report for each of his six small business clients. Each report used to take him about two hours.
Demonstrate.stock_query: man reviewing charts on laptop cafe
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Mateus · social media consultant · Porto Alegre

Demonstrate.voiceover: His template tells the AI it is an assistant to a social media consultant. The inputs are this month's figures, last month's figures, and his own notes. The format is a three-sentence summary, a comparison table, three observations, and two recommendations based only on his notes.

slide.title: Mateus's report template
slide.body: You are an assistant to a social media consultant who works with small local businesses. Write a monthly report for a [BUSINESS TYPE] client. Inputs: [FIGURES], [PREVIOUS FIGURES], [MY NOTES]. Format: 1) 3-sentence summary 2) table this month vs last 3) three observations 4) two recommendations, based only on my notes.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The rules are the most important part. Use only the figures I give. Do not calculate percentages unless I ask. Mark anything uncertain with the word check. And no marketing jargon. He removes client names and account details, and pastes only his exported figures and his own notes.

slide.title: The rules section
slide.body: Rules: use only the figures I give; do not calculate percentages unless I ask; mark anything uncertain with [CHECK]; no marketing jargon. Side note: client names and account details removed.

Demonstrate.voiceover: He records his times. The first draft takes about ten minutes. Then he spends about thirty-five minutes checking every figure against his source, rewriting the recommendations in his own words, and adding one idea for each client. That is his own measurement, on his own work.

slide.title: Mateus times his own work
slide.body: Simple timeline bar: Draft with template (about 10 min) → Check every figure, rewrite recommendations, add one client idea (about 35 min). Caption: his own measurement.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Notice this. The AI never decides what to recommend. It organises what Mateus already concluded. His expertise is in the observations and the recommendations. That is the part his clients pay for, and it stays with him.

A common mistake is to stop checking once the first few results are good. Templates reduce variation, but AI can still invent a figure or change a number. Keep the use only my inputs rule in every template, and check every number, every time.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a prompt template has five parts. Role and context, task, inputs, format and rules. Second, templates give you a consistent first draft for routine work. How much time they save depends on your task, so measure it yourself. Third, you keep the expert decisions and the final check, and you never put confidential client data into the inputs.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Role, task, inputs, format, rules. 2. Consistent first drafts; measure your own time saved. 3. You decide and check; no confidential data in the inputs.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise, choose your three most common deliverables and write a template for each, with all five parts. Test each one three times with example data. Then time one task with and without the template, including checking time. In the next lesson, we cover quality checks and client confidentiality.
